steps.title: The writing task at a glance
steps.intro: The first section of the test: one essay, 35 minutes, 25% of the Verbal Reasoning score.

tables.title: The rules
head: Rule
What it means
rows: One given task in a frame; the question is in bold at the end
At least 25 lines, at most 50 (the answer sheet); good essays: usually about 30-40 lines
10-23 lines: rated but marked as too short (points deducted); 0-9 lines: disqualified
Only on the lines; anything outside the lines, or after line 50, is not read
Pages in the test booklet; the draft is not marked; no extra answer sheet
Academic, well organized, clear and grammatically correct
Pencil (dark enough for the scanner) and eraser; legible, neat handwriting

tables.title: The scoring
head: Step
Score
rows: 25% of Verbal Reasoning (about a tenth of the general score)
Rated as a first draft written under time pressure

tables.title: The two rubrics
head: Content rubric
Language rubric
rows: Relevance to the task + a clear main idea
Critical thinking: precise definition of the issue, opinion vs fact, several perspectives, answering opposing views
Organizational tools: connectors, transition sentences, paragraphing (+ richness of vocabulary)

tips: You do not have to persuade: explain why you chose your position. Any position is legitimate.
Aim for 30-40 lines and never fewer than 25.
Stay exactly on the task: an off-topic essay gets the minimum.
Fly under the radar: if you are not sure of a word, use a simpler one you know.

steps.title: Academic register & hedging
steps.intro: Write like a calm, neutral narrator: formal, impersonal, qualified. Simple words are perfect.

tables.title: Informal → academic
head: Avoid
Write instead
rows: do not · it is · cannot · will not
children · many / much · the exact noun
get better · cut down on · find out
You can see that ... · We must ...
This shows that ... · The city should ...
In my opinion, I think ... · according to me
In my opinion, ... · I believe that ... · in my view
heartbreaking · a nightmare · a war zone
a proverb or a flowery image
what it means, in plain words

tables.title: Hedging words
head: Instead of (absolute)
Write (qualified)
rows: may · might · can · could · is likely to
often · in many cases · tends to
There is no doubt that · certainly

tips: Qualify the claims, not your position: the side you support stays clear.
One hedge per claim is enough: "might perhaps possibly" is foggy, not academic.
"May" does not repair a weak explanation; the reason still has to make sense.
Formal does not mean fancy: use only words you are 100% sure of.

steps.title: Precise word choice
steps.intro: Not 100% sure of a word or an expression? Let it go and say it plainly.

tables.title: The four precision errors
head: Error
Example → fix
rows: free reign → free rein (or: could act without fear of punishment)
the elitists → the elites · uniformity → unity
sportive time → time set aside for sport · moral veto → legitimate grounds
shoot themselves in the foot and publish → publish

tables.title: Hebrew-speaker traps
head: Avoid
Write
rows: In my opinion, ... / I think that ...
on the one side ... on the other side
on the one hand ... on the other hand
the opportunity to · the possibility of

tips: The same thing gets the same name all through the essay (face-recognition cameras ≠ security cameras).
Check the words that change the claim: suspect / criminal · reduce / eliminate · many / most · allow / require.
Look-alikes: affect / effect · economic / economical · sensible / sensitive · principal / principle.

steps.title: Grammar that changes meaning
steps.intro: Fix these first when you proofread: they change what your sentence says, or sound wrong to an academic reader.

tables.title: Errors and fixes
head: Problem
Wrong
Right
rows: the topic that the book deals with it
the topic that the book deals with
Citizens protest, the government will act.
If citizens protest, the government will act.
The council met the teachers; they rejected it.
Without cameras, the police can identify ...
Without cameras, the police cannot identify ...
easier access, to shorten and saving
easier access, shorter trips and savings

tables.title: Hebrew-speaker traps and style
head: Avoid
Write
rows: discuss about · explain me · depends in
discuss · explain to me · depends on
In my opinion I think / according to me
In my opinion, ... / I believe that ...
in case (= if) · being that · due to + clause
myself (as a subject) · whom (as a subject)
logical and reasonable · basically · a complex issue
say it once; delete empty words

tips: A few minor slips in a first draft will not sink you; errors that change the meaning will.
Keep one register through the whole essay: no single forced fancy phrase.
In proofreading, check every can / cannot, will / will not, more / less.
Unclear "this" or "they"?  Repeat the noun.

steps.title: Connectors by relationship
steps.intro: A connector signals a relationship; it does not create one. Decide the relationship first, then choose the word.

tables.title: Connectors
head: Relationship
Connectors
Note
rows: because · since · as · because of / due to
therefore · as a result · consequently · thus · which in turn
only if the link is explained
however · whereas · while · in contrast · on the other hand
although · even though · despite · admittedly ...; however · nevertheless
if · unless · provided that · as long as · only if
for example · for instance · such as · in particular
in conclusion · to sum up · in light of the above · overall

tables.title: Paragraph openers
head: Paragraph
Opens with
rows: no connector: In recent years, ... / Recently, ...
First, ... / To begin with, ... / First and foremost, ...
Second, ... / In addition, ... / Moreover, ... / Beyond this, ...
On the other hand, ... / Nevertheless, ... / Admittedly, ...
In conclusion, ... / To sum up, ... / In light of the above, ...

tips: Use only connectors you understand: albeit = although; "on the contrary" is not "on the other hand".
Turning a chain into a paragraph: each arrow gets a connector that names the link.
A new idea = a new paragraph; two arguments from the same field may share one.
No new line mid-paragraph; indent each new paragraph.

steps.title: Content rubric - what raters look for
steps.intro: Two raters, content 1-6 each (rated separately from language). A timed first draft - clarity of reasoning is what counts.

tables.title: The four content criteria
head: Criterion
What raters look for
Typical loss
rows: Answers the exact question, every part of it; a clear position; all reasons support it
A near miss (same topic, different question); reasons that point elsewhere
Varied arguments from different angles; full, logical explanations - every step from claim to result
Two reasons from the same angle; a missing link ("will reduce crime" with no route)
Each sentence adds something; a continuous line of thought; connectors that show the real relationship
The same idea in other words; padding; jumps; "Likewise" where contrast is needed
Precise issue; opinion vs fact (steps built from facts and reasonable assumptions); several perspectives; dealing with opposing views
Opinions stated as facts; one narrow angle; no answer to the other side

tables.title: Strong vs adequate vs weak
head: Feature
Strong
Adequate
Weak
rows: Stays with the exact decision and people
Changes the decision, people or setting
Reasons and position point different ways
Adds a step each sentence; the missing link is written
Names results, assumes the link, repeats
States its real reason fairly and answers that worry
Wording matches support; no invented facts

tips: Test: does each new sentence explain a cause, a consequence, a distinction, an illustration or a limit?
Examples explain a reason - they do not replace it, and one example does not show how common something is.
Length is not quality: 25-50 lines, good essays usually 30-40; more lines must mean more steps.

steps.title: Planning: analyse the task & find arguments
steps.intro: Before writing: analyse the task, gather what it gives you, choose a position you can explain, find arguments with three techniques, and test each one.

tables.title: 1 · Analyse the task
head: Ask
What to look for
rows: Friends with one aim, different ways, or rivals with different interests
The wider debate (cameras = security vs privacy)
Then it is often a clash of rights
Yes/no · degree (obvious or hidden: absolute end vs flexible end) · "why" (side chosen for you) · three opinions (ends + middle, or three different)
The decision · the people affected · the conditions. Do not drift to a different question.
Cover every element the question names (e.g. advantages AND disadvantages, for residents AND for the city)

tables.title: 2 · Gather from the task (2-3 minutes)
head: Part of the task
Where it goes
rows: Material for argument paragraphs, counter-arguments, weakenings
Keep you on the exact question; may become an argument or a weakening

tables.title: 3 · Choosing a position (considerations, not rules)
head: Consideration
Usually easier to explain
rows: The more moral side (e.g. protecting a vulnerable group)
Not changing it (but think again about an old law)
No extremes: the flexible end → a complex position with safeguards
The right the task explains in detail

tables.title: 4 · Three techniques for finding arguments
head: Technique
How
rows: Natural (life, liberty, movement, occupation, property, equality, dignity → privacy) · civil (vote, association, press, expression) · social (education, health, housing, work). Argue the harm is too great, or proportionate, in THIS task.
The wider frame + perspectives: economic · social · educational · psychological (+ moral, environmental, legal...) → how each affects each player
Who (the players) · what (possible benefit / harm) · how (the development). Who + what = the key sentence.

tables.title: 5 · The argument test
head: Test
Check
rows: Answers the exact question; does not dispute facts the task gives
The key sentence can be said in one breath
Draft the chain (~10 words): task → ... → result. Ask of every arrow "why would this lead to the next?"; add an explanation or condition; no arrows that just rename a step.
Write the opponent's chain; its weakest arrow = your weakening / rebuttal

tips: Aim for facts and reasonable assumptions, not only opinions; "in my opinion" goes only where the opinion starts.
Original angles (e.g. psychological) stand out, but only if they are explained as well as any other argument.
Practise finding arguments on published tasks, without always writing the whole essay.

steps.title: The chain
steps.intro: Draft a short cause → effect chain for each argument before you write it, test it, then turn every arrow into a sentence.

tables.title: How to draft it
head: Step
What to do
rows: The thing the task asks about (the exact policy or change)
The final result: the benefit or harm in your key sentence
Ask again and again: 'And what does that lead to?'
About 10 words per argument: a guide, not a limit
cameras installed → offenders know they are recorded → deterred → less crime in these areas

tables.title: The four checks
head: Check
How
rows: 'Why would this step lead to the next?' Weak arrow → add an explanation or a condition; broken arrow → add the missing step or drop the argument
'concentrate → pay attention' is the same thing twice: merge the boxes
Vary connectors and sentence shapes; never 'This will ... This will ...'
Draft the opponent's chain; its weakest arrow is your weakening

tables.title: Linking phrases for the arrows
head: Job
Phrases
rows: This, in turn, ...  ·  As a result, ...  ·  Consequently, ...  ·  This means that ...
..., which in turn ...  ·  ..., so that ...  ·  ..., leading to ...
as long as ...  ·  provided that ...  ·  if ...

tips: A connector signals a link; it does not create one. Make the arrow sound first.
Hedge the predictions: is likely to, would, may. Not 'will always'.

steps.title: Argument paragraph template
steps.intro: Key sentence → chain steps → (support) → closing link. Pick one phrase per slot and vary them.

tables.title: The slots
head: Slot
Options
rows: In my opinion, [X] should / should not [...], since it would [result].  ·  I believe that [X] should [...], as this is likely to [result].  ·  The main reason to support / oppose [X] is that ...
Once / When / If [X], [effect], because [reason].  ·  This, in turn, ...  ·  As a result, ...  ·  Consequently, ...  ·  This means that ...  ·  As long as [condition], ...
For example, a [person] who [...] would probably [...].  ·  A similar pattern can be seen in [similar field], where [...].
After support: In the same way, ...  ·  Similarly, ...  ·  Just as [...], so [...].  After development only: In this way, ...  ·  Thus, ...  ·  This is why ...

tables.title: Three versions
head: Template
Shape
rows: KEY · Once ... because ... · This, in turn, ... · As a result, ... · In this way, ...
KEY · When ... · Consequently, ..., which means that ... · For example, a ... who ... · In the same way, ...
KEY · If ... · As a result, ... · A similar pattern can be seen in ..., where ... · Just as ..., so ...

tips: The closing link mentions BOTH the support case and your own case; it never just repeats the key sentence.
No invented studies, statistics or experts. Well-known true facts: 'It is now well known that ...'.
Support is optional: key sentence + a fully explained chain can be a top-scoring paragraph.

steps.title: Rebuttal paragraph template
steps.intro: Before writing: draft THEIR chain (about 10 words), test every arrow, circle the weakest one. Then fill the four slots.

tables.title: The four slots
head: Slot
Job
Phrase options
rows: Contrast connector + their REASON (not just their side)
On the other hand, / However, / In contrast, + some argue that / opponents of ... claim that / it could be argued that ... because ...
Develop it as well as your own argument; they would sign it
since ... / this means that ... / as a result, ... / which in turn ... / In other words, the concern is that ...
3 · Our answer at the weak arrow
Reservation + weakening + explanation (+ support if there is room) + close
see the table below; then This is because ... / Moreover, ... / Therefore, [their worry] does not justify [their conclusion].
A small step toward them that eases the SAME worry, and says how
Nevertheless, / That said, + since [worry] is a legitimate concern, [measure] could be introduced, so that ...

tables.title: Weakening types
head: Type
Where it hits their chain
Reservation phrase
rows: Accepts the chain; the last box weighs less. Explain why IN THIS CASE (common good vs one person)
Admittedly, there is some truth in this; however, ... / Even if this is accepted, ...
However, this problem can be addressed by ...
A new branch (another problem), or a broken arrow: not true / not done / bypassed / exploited
However, ... may well lead to ... / At first glance, this seems convincing; however, it overlooks ...
Their own chain leads to the opposite result, in the SAME field
In fact, ... may have the opposite effect: ...

tips: Mentioning the other side is not answering it: state its reason and explain why that reason does or does not justify its conclusion.
Treat it fairly: never make it sound selfish or foolish.
Reply to its actual worry: what do they fear will happen, and how does your reply deal with that?
Weaken, do not refute; hedge (may, is likely to, many). "There is some logic in this", never "I understand them".
Avoid weak weakenings: the short blanket, extremism, the slippery slope.

steps.title: Bridging recommendation
steps.intro: Optional. At the end of the rebuttal paragraph, after the weakening: 80/20, not 50/50. Or, for strong writers, a complex position stated in the opening paragraph.

tables.title: Template
head: Part
Phrase options
rows: Nevertheless, / That said, / Even so, / At the same time,
since [their worry] is a legitimate concern, / since there is a genuine risk of ...,
[measure] could be introduced / should be accompanied by ... / it would be advisable to ... / could be limited to ...
so that ... / which would ensure that ... / In this way, [my position] would be kept while [the harm] would be reduced.
In my view, [position]; however, in light of [their worry], this should be done [with safeguard], as I will explain below.

tables.title: Check it
head: Question
Good sign
rows: Does it answer the SAME worry?
Cost worry → a cost measure (a free-dress Friday does not answer the cost of uniforms)
Does it say HOW it works?
Cameras: a dedicated body with sole access; every request examined before footage is viewed
It fixes a real weakness of your position, not a bone thrown to the other side
Exceptions stated openly ("all students, except those whose medical condition requires ..."), not a quiet contradiction

tips: A middle position has no automatic bonus: it must answer the question and fit your arguments.
"Both sides have a point" is not an answer.
Two nouns sharing one object need the same preposition: "a break-in to the database or a leak from it".

steps.title: Opening & closing templates
steps.intro: The bread of the sandwich: the opening comes from the task text, the closing from your own essay. Keep both short.

tables.title: Opening paragraph
head: Template
Fill in
rows: [Rewritten background: who is doing what, and why]. However, some oppose this [move / proposal], and I [agree with them / believe it should nevertheless be adopted].
[Every sentence of the task text, shortened]. Supporters argue that [...]. Opponents, however, fear that [...]. I agree with the [former / latter], [although / provided that ...].
I agree with the former. · I side with the critics. · In my view, [X] should [not] be [adopted].

tables.title: Closing paragraph
head: Template
Fill in (and where each part comes from)
rows: In conclusion, [position = last line of the opening], since [benefit 1 = second half of key sentence 1], and also because [benefit 2 = second half of key sentence 2].
In conclusion, although [counterargument = first line of the rebuttal], I believe that [position], since [weakening]. Moreover, [benefit 1], and [benefit 2].
In conclusion, [position], since, as shown above, its advantages outweigh its disadvantages.

tips: Opening: background + dispute + your position (at the end). About 2-3 minutes. No empty phrases ("This is a problematic issue").
Copying segments of the task text is fine, but not the whole task word for word. Struggling to rewrite? Use the minimal template.
Closing: no new argument, no repeated counterargument. It must follow from the body.
Never leave out the closing. No time? The one-line template.

steps.title: Essay skeleton + 35-minute plan
steps.intro: Plan the content first (short notes and chains), then write. Opening and closing are not in the skeleton: their content is known.

tables.title: The skeleton (basic structure 1)
head: Paragraph
Write in the skeleton
rows: Argument + chain (~10 words: X -> step -> step -> result) + example or comparison
A different reason + chain + example or comparison
Counterargument (their chain) + weakening: a NEW argument aimed at their weakest arrow
Relevance to the exact question · flow in the whole essay · every arrow: "why would this lead to that?"

tables.title: 35 minutes
head: Minutes
Stage
rows: Read, analyse, find arguments and weakenings, choose a side, skeleton + chains

tips: Argument 2 needed for the weakening? Basic structure 2: drop argument paragraph 2, richer rebuttal, longer opening.
Always short on time? Opening -> argument 1 -> rebuttal -> (argument 2 if time) -> closing.
The structure is a teaching aid, not an exam rule: let the task shape the paragraphs, and give each paragraph one job.
Length: at least 25 lines, at most 50; good essays are usually about 30-40.

steps.title: Proofreading checklist
steps.intro: 2-3 minutes at the end (or one quick check after each paragraph). Raters read a first draft: fix language, not content.

tables.title: Check
head: What
Look for
rows: Full stops · comma after an opening phrase · no comma splices
Subject-verb (the cameras are) · singular/plural · pronouns (this data ... it)
Each example or comparison ends by tying back to the topic
The same idea in other words: cross the sentence out
A missing link between sentences: add the connector that fits the relationship
Go first to the paragraph that felt weaker while writing

tips: Leave a blank line between paragraphs and indent each first line: room for corrections.
Delete with one clean line; insert with a caret (^). Keep it clear.
Write only on the lines, in pencil, legibly: an illegible essay gets the lowest score.
A few small mistakes are fine. It is a draft.

steps.title: Practice writing tasks
steps.intro: Eight original tasks in the style of the exam. Write each one in 35 minutes, on a 50-line sheet.

tables.title: Tasks
head: Task
rows: Several cities have closed their centres to private cars, allowing only buses, bicycles and delivery vehicles. Supporters say that the change reduces pollution and noise and makes streets safer for pedestrians. Shop owners and residents of outlying neighbourhoods worry that fewer customers will come and that reaching the centre will become harder. In your opinion, should city centres be closed to private cars? Give reasons.

Some countries require every high-school student to complete a set number of hours of community volunteering before graduating. Supporters believe that the requirement teaches responsibility and connects young people with their community. Critics argue that volunteering loses its value when it is compulsory and that the hours take time away from studies. In your opinion, should community volunteering be a graduation requirement? Give reasons.

A number of cities have made public buses free for all residents, funding the service from municipal taxes. Supporters say that free buses encourage people to leave their cars at home and help low-income families. Opponents point out that the cost falls on all taxpayers, including those who never use the buses, and that the money could improve the service instead. In your opinion, should public transport in cities be free? Give reasons.

More and more schools require students to hand in their smartphones at the start of the school day. Supporters say that phones distract students in class and encourage online bullying during breaks. Some parents and students object that phones are useful learning tools and that parents need to be able to reach their children. In your opinion, should smartphones be banned during the school day? Give reasons.

Several governments have introduced a special tax on sweetened drinks. Supporters argue that a higher price reduces the consumption of sugar and that the income can fund health programmes. Opponents claim that the tax mainly burdens low-income families and that adults should make their own choices about what they drink. In your opinion, is a tax on sweetened drinks a good policy? Give reasons.

Hospital emergency rooms are often crowded with patients whose problems are not urgent. Some hospitals have proposed charging a fee to patients who come to the emergency room without a referral and are found not to need urgent care. Supporters believe that the fee would shorten waiting times for those in real danger. Critics warn that some people might stay at home even when they are seriously ill. In your opinion, should such a fee be introduced? Give reasons.

In some primary schools, teachers have stopped giving homework altogether. Those in favour say that young children need free time to play and rest, and that homework widens the gap between children who get help at home and those who do not. Others believe that homework builds independent study habits and lets parents follow what their children are learning. In your opinion, should homework in primary schools be abolished? Give reasons.

In popular tourist cities, many apartments are rented to tourists for short stays instead of to local residents. Some cities have limited the number of days a year an apartment may be rented this way. Supporters say that the limit returns homes to the market and lowers rents for residents. Opponents argue that it harms owners who depend on the income and reduces the money tourists bring to the city. In your opinion, which is more important: protecting residents' access to housing, or allowing owners to rent freely? Give reasons.

tips: How to practise: set a timer for 35 minutes. Spend the first 8-10 minutes on the skeleton: draft a chain (~10 words) for each argument and for the opponent's main argument, and find its weakest arrow.
Then write on a 50-line sheet (at least 25 lines; about 30-40 is good), and leave 2-3 minutes to check with the proofreading checklist.
Note the time of every stage. A day later, review the essay (key lines first, then paragraph by paragraph), fix it, and only then submit it.
Best of all: write the same task again from the other side.
